title: History Repeats Itself: Government’s Role in the Market
content:
What affects the market? The answer: everything. To start, let’s analyze how the government and its actions throughout the years have caused boom and bust cycles in the market. From the Federal Reserve’s interest rate calls to government policies to political tensions, the government has the capability to swing the market in an instant. To “beat” the market, smart investors constantly look at the news and find trends for what the governments of the world might do next. Many people are worried that there may be another stock market crash coming in the next few months. To look at the present, we must look at the past.
To start, the most recent economic disaster was the 2008 Financial Crisis. Leading up to the disaster, the government began deregulating. The Glass-Steagall Repeal (1999) led commercial banks to combine with investment banks, leading to a huge interconnected network between banks. Additionally, the Commodity Futures Modernization Act (2000) exempted CDS from regulation: CDS is a form of unregulated insurance that was used for loans and eventually was a contributing factor to lending problems.
A bubble in the stock market is a huge surge of prices that overestimates the actual value of the stocks, which could be seen with the housing bubble that resulted in the 2008 crash. However, the less-known 2001 Dot-Com crash, with the rise of the internet, caused Alan Greenspan (Federal Reserve leader) to drop interest rates massively from 6.5% to 1%. This massive cut allowed people to constantly borrow and let more money circulate in the economy. Despite this sounding like a positive, the cost of purchasing a house dropped, leaving millions of people to buy a home that drove prices for houses up, classic supply and demand. Mortgages that were given to high-risk borrowers, borrowers who were more likely not to pay, were widespread due to the rising demand, and the market was bound to collapse. But the banks were “too big to fail”, right?
As inflation continued to rise, the Federal Reserve decided to raise interest rates back down to 5.25% by the end of 2007. There was then a huge increase in housing availability, subsequently dropping housing prices across the country that destroyed the capital reserves of the banks. The government quickly responded by providing emergency loans to US banks, and the interest rates were slashed to near-zero rates. After the economy recovered through the government and central bank’s help, there were policies put into place to ensure it would never occur again. Congress passed the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform that created the Volcker Rule, stopping commercial banks from investing using their own money, and SIFIs and the CFPB were established to intervene in the market. 
The 2008 stock market crash taught investors a lot of important information applicable today. For instance, interest rates were seen to hike over the past years after extremely low interest rates to reduce inflation. The government also ensured that major banks have regulations on them regularly. Major events such as the one in 2008 and even the Great Depression impact the market today and force investors to think differently, so whenever you are speculating future investments, always consider past trends.
Let’s look at another example of the government’s consequences on the market. Increasing amounts of corn-based fuel (biofuel) have become a popular movement, along with other renewable resources that don’t use crude oil or non-renewable resources. Congress mandated that these fuel sources can be used, requiring refiners to have corn ethanol in the gas and to prove themselves with what are called RINs (Renewable Identification Numbers).
This mandate federally forces farmers to move from crops such as soybeans and wheat (that are prominent in the Midwest) to corn. Corn today remains the most popular crop that is farmed in the United States. As a result, corn bushels moved from $2.00 to $8.00 from the early 2000 to 2012, spiking costs and demand. Additionally, with more corn being grown and taking up land, there is a reduction in other agricultural goods. The prices of wheat and soybeans surged, hurting the everyday consumer who purchased products such as bread. The changes in the stock market weren’t only in crops, though; there was an influx of fertilizer stocks, such as MOS’s increase (until the 2008 crash). 
Oil stocks also dropped because of a noticeable shift towards renewable methods, and shifting slightly away from oil by mixing corn ethanol into their product. Indirectly, cattle such as pigs, chickens, and cows all suffered from the rising costs of crops. It requires more money to maintain the animals for slaughter, which increases food prices for almost the entire food industry. These seemingly small changes in policies made by the government can quickly form ripples in the entire stock market: you just have to look for them.
Both the 2008 stock market crash and the corn policy show that a prudent investor will always be monitoring the news, as anything can impact the market at any point.

title: “Accept All Cookies”: The World’s Most Frequently Signed Lie
content:
Do British people receive biscuits instead? Sadly, no – and neither do you, no matter how many times a website politely asks if it can give you some “cookies”. It’s one of the most confusing pieces of internet jargon out there: a word that makes you think of an afternoon snack, attached to a little pop-up banner that appears on basically every website you visit. So what is actually happening when you click “Accept”? As it turns out, the answer is much less mysterious – and much less delicious – than it sounds.
What Is a Cookie, Really?
Strip away the cute name, and a cookie is just a small text file. According to the UK’s Information Commissioner’s Office, it’s a small file of letters and numbers that gets downloaded onto your device the moment you visit a website, and it can do things like remembering your preferences, keeping track of what’s in your shopping basket, or simply counting how many visitors a page has had. Ireland’s Data Protection Commission describes it the same way – a small text file stored on your computer, phone, or even a smart TV, letting a website remember who you are and what you were doing the last time you dropped by.
The name itself is oddly charming considering how unglamorous the technology is. It traces back to an old computing term called a “magic cookie” – a packet of data passed between programs without being changed – which a web developer borrowed in 1994 to solve a very unromantic problem: an online store’s servers were getting overloaded and needed a way to remember shoppers without storing everything centrally.
How Do Cookies Actually Work?
Think of visiting a website for the first time as walking into a big department store where nobody knows you. The moment you walk in, a greeter hands you a small numbered tag. You don’t think twice about it – you just slip it in your pocket. Now, as you wander from the fitting room to the café to the checkout counter, every single desk you pass can glance at your tag and instantly know who you are and what you were doing a moment ago. You never have to explain yourself twice.
That numbered tag is exactly what a cookie is. When you first land on a website, its server quietly hands your browser a small piece of data – basically a random ID – and your browser tucks it away. From then on, every time you click to a new page on that same site, your browser automatically shows that same tag again, without you doing anything at all. The website reads it and picks up right where you left off: still logged in, cart still full, preferences still remembered.
Kaspersky’s security team compares this to a coat check at a restaurant: you hand over your coat (your data), you get a numbered ticket back (the cookie), and later that ticket is all the desk needs to hand your coat straight back – no explanation required. And just like that ticket only works at the one restaurant that issued it, a cookie only works on the website that created it. Walk into a completely different store, and your old tag means nothing there – that website has never seen you before and will hand you a brand new one of its own.
A few small details decide how long a tag lasts and how far it travels: some tags are only good for today and get thrown out the moment you leave (these disappear when you close your browser), while others are built to last for weeks or months so the site remembers you next time you visit.
What Are Cookies Actually Used For?
Cookies quietly power a huge amount of what feels “smart” about the modern web. The three big jobs, as both the ICO and Kaspersky describe them, are:
Staying logged in: Without a cookie holding your session, every new page you clicked would look like your very first visit — you’d have to log in again and again.
Remembering your choices: Language settings, themes, and items sitting in a shopping cart all typically live in a cookie so the site doesn’t forget them the moment you navigate away.
Tracking and personalizing: Cookies can quietly note which pages and products you’ve looked at, which is how sites end up recommending things you might like — or, less charmingly, how advertisers build a profile of your browsing habits.
Session Cookies vs. Persistent Cookies (and First-Party vs. Third-Party)
Not all cookies are built to last. Session cookies live only as long as your browser tab is open; close it, and they vanish, which is why re-opening your browser sometimes logs you out of things. Persistent cookies are built to stick around, often with a specific expiry date, so a site can recognize you days or months later without you having to sign in again each time.
There’s a second, equally important split: first-party cookies, set directly by the website you’re actually visiting, and third-party cookies, set by some other domain – usually an advertiser or analytics company embedded on that page. First-party cookies tend to be the harmless, functional kind. Third-party cookies are the ones responsible for that slightly unsettling experience of an ad following you around the internet after you looked at one pair of shoes.
The Legal Side: Why Every Site Asks Your Permission
Those “we use cookies” banners aren’t just good manners – they’re the law. In the UK, cookie use is governed by the Privacy and Electronic Communications Regulations, enforced by the ICO, which requires organizations to clearly explain how they use cookies and to give you a genuine way to consent before setting anything that isn’t strictly necessary for the site to function. Ireland’s Data Protection Commission enforces similar rules under EU data protection law, noting that cookies can be used for everything from keeping your shopping cart intact to authenticating your access to your online banking – which is exactly why regulators care about how transparently they’re used.
Practically, this is why clicking “Accept” or “Reject” on that banner actually does something: rejecting non-essential cookies is supposed to stop advertising and tracking cookies from being set, while the essential ones that keep the site working are typically allowed to persist either way.
Are Cookies Dangerous?
Mostly, no. A cookie is a small text file, not a program – it can’t run code, install anything, or reach into your files. But that doesn’t mean cookies are entirely without risk. Because third-party tracking cookies can build up a surprisingly detailed picture of your browsing habits over time, they’ve become one of the main tools behind targeted advertising and cross-site profiling. There’s also a nastier cousin worth knowing about: so-called “zombie” or “supercookies”, which are designed to reappear even after you think you’ve deleted them, and which security researchers flag as far harder to get rid of than an ordinary cookie.
How to Take Control of Your Cookies
You don’t need to memorize any of the technical details above to manage this sensibly. A few practical habits:
Use the cookie banner deliberately. Rejecting non-essential cookies where you’re offered the choice generally cuts down on tracking without breaking the site.
Check your browser’s cookie settings. Every major browser lets you view, block, or clear cookies, and most let you specifically block third-party cookies while leaving first-party ones alone.
Use private or incognito browsing for one-off visits. It won’t make you invisible, but it stops cookies from that session persisting afterward.
Clear cookies periodically, especially on shared or public computers, since a lingering session cookie is effectively a way of staying logged into your accounts.
The Bottom Line
A cookie is nothing more than a small file letting a website remember a fact about your visit – the digital equivalent of a coat-check ticket. That’s genuinely useful: it’s the reason you don’t have to log in every time you click a new page, and the reason your shopping cart doesn’t reset itself out of nowhere. The part worth paying attention to isn’t the cookie itself, but who’s allowed to read it – a first-party cookie remembering your language preference is a very different thing from a third-party cookie quietly building a profile of everywhere you’ve clicked. So no, the banner isn’t offering you a snack. But now you know exactly what it is offering, and that’s a much better trade.

title: Lake America: US-Canada Trade War
content:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, on August 22, 2026, stated that Canada was “at war” with the United States over trade. This was in response to the trade talks that broke down between the two nations the week before. As a result, the US imposed 50% tariffs on numerous goods. Carney then responded with “a match, dollar for dollar”. President Trump stated that Canada has been acting unreasonably and posted on social media that Canada wants the benefits of being a U.S. state without being one. But can we really call this a war?
Tariffs are a form of import tax, meaning any goods that are brought into the country will be taxed, and the purpose of tariffs is to both bring in more cash and to promote large companies to begin manufacturing domestically to further build the economy. However, tariffs have seen both successes and failures in the history of the United States. For instance, tariffs were a major source of income during the 18th century, while the Tariff Act of 1930 resulted in further repercussions during the Great Depression.
The US and Canadian economies have been interlocked for decades with supply chain integration and energy flow. In fact, Canada’s largest trade partner is the US, and Canada is the United States’s second largest trade partner behind Mexico. Due to the US, Canada, and Mexico’s economies being so reliant on one another, the three countries have been, for the most part, tariff-free because of the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA). 
During President Trump’s first term, he wanted NAFTA to be renegotiated, leading to the United States-Mexico-Canada Trade Agreement (USMCA). The main differences are the stricter labor laws and regional requirements in the automobile industry. In his second term, the President announced large tariffs on Canada along with global tariffs on metals (steel, aluminum). Canada, in response, placed tariffs on the US.
US-Canada tariffs have had times of progress and when talks were stymied. President Trump also was forced to rework the legal basis of his tariffs after a Supreme Court ruling in early 2026. Last month in July, he put 50% tariffs on over 20 billion dollars worth of Canadian goods consisting of cement, wine, and hockey sticks, and he did so because he said Canada unfairly discriminated against US goods such as cars, dairy, and alcohol. Therefore, many Canadian suppliers have stopped sales of US alcohol. The two countries had talks, almost reaching a deal, but then ultimately led to the implementation of these tariffs. 
Canada, of course, had to respond with their own tariffs, which are set to be executed on September 8th, 2026, on over 700 products. The three main demands that led to Canada backing off on the deal with the US were automotive tariff relief, limiting Canada’s capability to trade with other countries, and the United States’s attempt to undermine Canada’s sovereignty. The United States’s reasons include drug trafficking, unfair trade, and wildfire smoke.
The results of the trade war caused an effect on both nations. The US tariffs would affect 5% of imports and result in rises in both inflation and unemployment levels. According to the Yale Budget Lab, U.S. tariffs would cost every American household over a thousand dollars. In general, trade wars hurt the economy by reducing supply, and therefore increasing the demand for products. It is not all gloom and doom, however; U.S. tariffs brought in over 200 billion dollars for the US Federal Government, and many corporations have moved to the US from other countries for their manufacturing and production. The large influx of capital can result in developments in other sectors of the economy, society, or offset the Iranian war.
Additionally, President Trump threatens to rename Lake Ontario to “Lake America”, claiming that he was not joking, and the same initiative was seen in early 2025 with the Gulf of Mexico being changed to the Gulf of America. Recently, he signed an executive order declaring Lake America, appearing on Google Maps for US residents, stirring up mixed feelings about the change. President Trump also continuously talks about Canada becoming the 51st state, angering Canadians. These actions have sparked the Canadian people to be in favor of imposing tariffs on the United States, with a large 74% majority in favor of doing so. The liberal party in Canada, run by the current Prime Minister, has also gained popularity by promoting Canadian sovereignty. This symbolizes the looming threat and escalating tensions between the two nations.
Along with the conflict in Iran, the US-Canada trade war has further been exacerbated as they harm the economy and households as inflation continues to rise. In July, the country lost 23,000 jobs, which was unexpected, in addition to revising the previous two months down by more than 100,000 jobs. Even though the unemployment rate dropped from 4.2% to 4.1% in the last month, it is important to note that the rate only accounts for people searching for jobs, so fewer people are actually looking for jobs, leading to a reduction in the economy’s health. Inflation has seen a rise of 3.5%, higher than the wage growth of 3.2%, meaning that workers, on average, are getting a smaller pay each year due to these conflicts. So, to answer the question if this is war: yes, but it’s complicated.

title: The Difference Between You and a Cliff-Diver
content:
There’s always that one friend who’s the first to propose a spontaneous night drive in the group chat, who’s down for any adventure, no matter the time, date, or place. And then there’s the yin to their yang, who responds to that same proposal with four follow-up questions and a 2 page argument against the idea. Somehow, you end up going anyway, dragged along by the treacherous group consensus, while the second friend details every possible thing that could go wrong the entire car drive.
This is usually explained away with personality talk- one of the friends is just “spontaneous” and “adventure-loving,” and the other is “just anxious”, but what’s actually going on has less to do with who’s a party animal and who’s a party pooper and more to do with two brain systems that are running on different clocks.
The ventral striatum is a deceptively small structure buried in the depths of your brain, and is the ‘first responder’ of your reward system. The instant that something promising shows up, like a good deal, an unexpectedly high score, this part of your brain reacts first. On the other hand, the prefrontal cortex that sits right behind your forehead works on a much slower timeline by gathering information, running the odds, and checking for a catch before it lets you commit to anything. Risk-based decision-making relies on the coordination between different brain regions, as the prefrontal cortex handles big-picture thinking while the striatum pushes you towards reward. (Zhao et al.,2025)
In more impulsive brains, the connection between the reward system and prefrontal cortex tends to be relatively weaker, so the signal advising towards patience and weighing the consequences before the decision takes more time to arrive, and by the time it has, you’re already halfway up the cliff. To put it in layman’s terms, impulsive brains have brakes too, but the accelerator always beats it to the race.
On the other hand, cautious decision-makers’ brains have been proven to have increased levels of activity in a particular region of the prefrontal cortex called the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, which acts as the control center for self-control. When researchers experimentally increased this area’s activity up or down, people’s willingness to take a gamble on uncertain outcomes shifted with it. (Wagner et al., 2022)  Differences in your brain’s fronto-striatal wiring have been directly linked to how impulsive someone tends to be. (Kaur & Sohal, 2025)
Dopamine is usually blamed for impulsivity, but the link between risk-taking and dopamine is closer related to the availability of your body’s dopamine receptors rather than the amount of dopamine you have in your body.  Lower availability of a specific kind of dopamine receptor has been tied to greater risk-taking. (Gianaros et al., 2015)
It’s important to remember that this doesn’t make one type of brain better than the other. Impulsive brains are the reason some people make the leap into founding a company nobody else believed in, or making the split-second call that can win a game. Cautious brains are the reason surgeons don’t rush a procedure, scientists triple-check their data before publishing, and some people never end up with a regrettable tattoo from 2 am on a whim. Every functional group project needs both kinds of people in it.
This wiring in your brain isn’t permanent either- during adolescence, the reward-driven systems in your brain mature much faster than the regulatory prefrontal systems, and this mismatch, amplified by a surge in dopamine activity, is a large part of why teenagers tend to run more impulsively than adults do. This gap narrows gradually as the prefrontal cortex keeps developing into your mid-twenties, which is also why the friend proposing spontaneous night drives at 17 isn’t guaranteed to be the same person at 30.

title: What’s Up with the Debt Crisis?
content:
The bond market is widely considered one of the most secure forms of investment. Bonds are a form of security that is long-term debt where the issuer is obliged to pay regular interest to the holder and repay the principal at maturity. In essence, it is a loan that you give in hopes of getting paid back your money and some extra. The bond market is 30% larger compared to the equity market in terms of market capitalization. People who begin to reach retirement age are more likely to buy bonds, which helps them keep their money safe compared to the stock market.
This form of investment is extremely safe with the US government and a huge corporation that you may be lending to. One of the only risks is that the lender is unable to repay (defaulting) the loan, usually through bankruptcy, which is why companies pay a higher yield compared to the government as an incentive. The longer someone provides the loan, the more interest that they obtain because if the money stays with the company longer, it is a higher risk that the loaner must consider, in addition to money that could be used for other uses or securities. Bond prices and yields are inversely proportional: when interest rates go up, bond prices drop. Bonds are measured through a scale, and they are given a rating from independent groups like Moody’s, Standard & Poor’s, and Fitch, all having their individualized methods of rating. Historically, the US government was the gold standard for bonds, but in the last decade, the US government bonds saw a slight decline in their ratings, from the highest AAA/Aaa to a lower grade. While this may not seem substantial, it is a signal for a larger shift in the market.
The US government’s debt has climbed to 40 trillion dollars for the first time in the country’s history because of persistent government budget deficits (borrowing more than collecting in revenue), double that of a decade earlier at around 20 trillion. Some factors that are contributing to this debt are from Social Security, Medicare, and other necessary expenditures. To put that into perspective, the national debt is higher than the worth of every single-family home in the United States. The interest from the debt alone is more than 1.2 trillion, spending more on interest than national defense. Eventually, if the federal government continues to add to this debt, then there would be a very serious economic crisis through either hyperinflation or high interest rates. America’s long-term borrowing cost, also known as the rate of return that investors demand, hit the highest levels since the Great Financial Crisis.
Scott Bessent, US Secretary of the Treasury, bought back long-term debt to borrow more short-term debt instead. The 30-Year Treasury bond yield fell by around 0.1 percent to around 5.19%, which is substantial in the bond market. To visualize the effect that it will have on the market, imagine that the bond market has suddenly experienced a large surge of people who want their money back from these loans, backed by big-tech companies who ordered billions more for AI. These investments in AI have already caused turmoil and uncertainty in the markets, as the volatility of AI endeavors appears as time goes on. Additionally, oil is above 90 dollars, and inflation is still high from the Iranian conflict, contributing to surge pricing. Therefore, lenders want more money upfront for longer bonds due to the rising risk of the value of currency in the future. This concept is known as TVM or, more specifically, Inflation Risk Premium, as a dollar today can be worth more than a dollar in the future because today’s money can earn both interest and avoid inflation.
Bessent is attempting to wait out the market by having shorter-term debt in hopes the rates go down, but if they don’t due to the constant high inflation from the war, it can further lead to complications in the future. The compounding of interest would have severe consequences and can be similarly seen in credit card interest rates, which grow exponentially in a bank through compounding. Bessent himself condemned this strategy when he criticized the previous Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen for doing the same plan of action.
In recent years, under both the Trump and Biden administrations, the national debt consistently rises throughout the years, and the lack of leadership in Congress and the government in general is what many say is to blame for the debt crisis. For instance, most Congressmen do not focus on the national debt, and only a select few were supporting spending cuts to reduce the federal debt. However, as the problem escalates, if the issue is not addressed, there would be more drastic spending cuts and possible tax increases to bring back the debt to a manageable level. Lisa Desjardins further stated that if the trend persists without anyone discussing remedies, the debt may increase to $50 trillion in the next few years.

title: The Future of AI: AI Agent
content:
Chances are, when you think of “AI”, a chat window pops into your head. You type a question, it types back an answer, and that’s it. That’s how most people met AI, and for years, it’s mostly what AI was.
But something is shifting. The most interesting AI tools being built today don’t just answer – they act. They check your inbox, pull data from your tools, draft the reply, and even schedule the follow-up, all without you sitting there typing prompt after prompt. This is the world of AI agents, and it’s quickly becoming clear that this – not the chatbot – is where AI is actually headed.
This article breaks down what an AI agent really is, how it’s different from a chatbot, why that difference matters, and where things are going next.
What Is an AI Agent, Really?
Google Cloud puts it simply: AI agents are software systems that use AI to pursue goals and complete tasks on behalf of users. They show reasoning, planning, and memory, and have a level of autonomy to make decisions, learn, and adapt.
The key word there is autonomy. A chatbot waits for you to say something, then responds. An agent, on the other hand, can be given a goal – like “find the biggest drop-off point in our signup funnel” – and it will figure out the steps needed to get there on its own: pulling data, analyzing it, drawing a conclusion, and even taking action, all without you walking it through each step.
Think of the difference this way:
A chatbot is like a very knowledgeable person standing behind a counter, only ever answering the exact question you ask.
An agent is like an employee you can hand a task to, who goes off, does the research, checks with the right systems, and comes back with a finished result – or a draft ready for your approval.
Chatbot vs. Assistant vs. Agent: What’s the Actual Difference?
These terms get thrown around loosely, so it helps to separate them clearly. Google Cloud frames it as a spectrum of autonomy.
Chatbot	AI Assistant	AI Agent
Purpose	Automating simple tasks or conversations	Assisting users with tasks	Autonomously and proactively performing tasks
How it acts	Follows pre-defined rules, limited learning	Responds to requests, can recommend actions, but you make the final call	Can perform complex, multi-step actions and make decisions independently
Interaction style	Reactive – responds to triggers	Reactive – responds to your prompts	Proactive – works toward a goal
A basic chatbot follows scripted rules and can’t really learn. An AI assistant, like the chat window most people are used to, is smarter and more conversational, but it still waits for you to ask, and you’re the one deciding what happens next. An agent flips that relationship: you set the goal, and it plans and executes the steps, often looping through multiple actions before checking back in with you.
How Does an Agent Actually “Think” and Work?
Under the hood, most AI agents run on the same basic loop, often described using a framework called ReAct – short for reasoning and acting. Here’s roughly what that loop looks like:
Observe: the agent gathers information about the situation, whether that’s reading an email, checking a database, or scanning a support ticket.
Reason: it uses that information to figure out what’s going on and what should happen next, similar to how a person thinks through a problem before acting.
Plan: it maps out the steps needed to reach the goal, and reconsiders the plan if something unexpected comes up.
Act: it actually does something: sends a message, updates a spreadsheet, opens a support ticket, or calls another tool.
Refine: over time, agents can learn from what worked and what didn’t, adjusting how they handle similar situations in the future.
To pull this off, agents typically combine a few core building blocks. A large language model acts as the “brain”, handling language and reasoning. Memory lets the agent remember what happened earlier in a task, or even across many past runs, instead of starting from zero every time. And tools are the hands – connections to apps like email, calendars, spreadsheets, or company databases that let the agent actually do things in the real world, not just talk about them.
One practical piece worth knowing about: many agent platforms now use “skills” – small, focused packages of instructions for one specific job, like validating an expense report or drafting a customer reply. Instead of cramming every possible instruction into one giant prompt, the agent keeps a catalog of these narrow skills and only pulls up the relevant one when a task actually matches it. This keeps the agent focused and makes it much easier for a team to update just one part of its behavior without breaking everything else.
Working Solo or as a Team
Agents don’t always work alone. Google Cloud distinguishes between single-agent and multi-agent systems:
Single agents operate independently on a well-defined task — for example, one agent dedicated entirely to monitoring a sales pipeline.
Multi-agent systems involve several agents working together, each with a different specialty, collaborating or even debating to reach a better outcome. One agent might research a topic, hand its findings to a second agent that drafts content, which is then reviewed by a third.
This teamwork mirrors how human teams operate: a researcher, a writer, and an editor each doing their part before the finished product comes together. Multi-agent setups can also run in the background – sometimes called autopilots – running on a schedule or reacting to events, without a person needing to kick things off each time.
Where Are Agents Already Being Used?
This isn’t a far-off, theoretical idea – agents are already doing real work across industries. Google Cloud groups common use cases into a handful of broad categories:
Customer agents handle support conversations, answer questions, and recommend products, working across chat, phone, or a company’s app.
Employee agents take repetitive internal work off people’s plates — managing schedules, drafting internal communications, or answering routine employee questions.
Creative agents help generate content, ideas, and campaign drafts.
Data agents dig through company data to surface insights, like spotting exactly where users are dropping off in a signup process.
Code agents assist developers by writing, reviewing, and speeding up software work.
Security agents watch for threats and speed up how quickly a team can investigate and respond to an incident.
In everyday business terms, this looks like an agent that watches a support inbox and drafts replies automatically, one that scans a company’s sales pipeline every morning and flags stalled deals, or one that reviews open code changes and nudges the right teammate when something’s been sitting too long. The common thread is always the same: instead of a person doing the repetitive middle step, the agent handles it and hands back a result – or a decision – ready for a quick human check.
The Case for Agents Over Chatbots
So why does this shift matter? A few clear advantages keep coming up:
They finish the job, not just the conversation. A chatbot can tell you how to do something. An agent can actually go and do it – pulling real data, taking real actions, and reporting back with results instead of instructions.
They save real time. Tasks that used to require a person to manually check five different tools, copy data between them, and write a summary can now be handled from start to finish while that person focuses on something that actually needs human judgment.
They get sharper with more context. Because agents can hold onto memory and connect to a company’s actual tools and documents, their answers and actions become more accurate and relevant over time, instead of relying only on generic knowledge.
They can work as a team. Multiple agents, each handling one part of a bigger job, can tackle more complex workflows than a single chatbot ever could on its own.
What Agents Still Can’t Do Well
It’s worth being honest about the limits, too. Google Cloud points to a few areas where agents still struggle:
Deep empathy and nuanced human interaction: tasks like therapy, social work, or conflict resolution need a level of emotional understanding that AI doesn’t have yet.
High-stakes ethical decisions: in areas like healthcare diagnoses, law enforcement, or judicial decisions, agents lack the judgment and moral reasoning these situations demand.
Unpredictable physical environments: tasks like surgery or disaster response need real-time physical adaptation that today’s agents can’t reliably handle.
Cost and complexity: building and running sophisticated agents can be resource-intensive, which can put them out of reach for smaller teams or tighter budgets.
Because of this, agents work best as a layer that handles the repetitive, well-defined parts of a job – with a person still reviewing anything sensitive, high-stakes, or ambiguous before it’s finalized. Most agent platforms are built with this in mind, keeping a human approval step before an agent’s proposed action actually goes live.
Will Agents Replace Chatbots Completely?
Probably not entirely – but the role of the simple chatbot is shrinking. Chat will likely stick around as the front door: the easiest way for a person to explain what they need in plain language. But behind that chat window, the actual work is increasingly being handed off to agents that can reason, plan, and take multi-step action, rather than a script that can only answer the exact question it was asked.
In practice, the two are merging. Ask an agent-based system a question today, and instead of just getting an answer, you might get a finished analysis, a drafted email, or a ticket already created for your team – with the conversation simply being how you kicked it off. The chatbot becomes the interface; the agent becomes the actual worker behind it.
Looking Ahead
The direction is fairly clear: as AI models get better at reasoning and as tools get easier to connect, agents will keep taking on more of the tedious, multi-step work that used to require a person clicking through five different apps. Multi-agent teams – where specialized agents hand tasks to each other – are likely to become the norm for anything beyond simple, single-step requests. And rather than being locked to one company’s chatbot, agents are increasingly designed to plug into whatever tools a team already uses, from email and calendars to sales and support platforms.
None of this means chatbots disappear. It means the conversation becomes the starting point, not the whole product. The real value shifts to what happens after you hit send – whether the system just talks back, or actually goes and gets the job done.

title: 5 More Minutes And Other Lies Your Brain Tells You
content:
You’ve been studying for over an hour straight. As you get up and stretch lazily, you reach for your phone, for a quick 5-minute break. 1 hour later, you finally surface from a never-ending hole of doomscrolling with no thoughts in your head, woken by your mom calling you down for dinner. Sounds familiar? This is the life of almost every teenager with access to social media.
Social media addiction is easily attributed to “teenage laziness, weak will, or a lack of discipline”, but in reality, these misconceptions obscure the much more complex neuroscience of the pull of social media.
The nucleus accumbens is a structure in your brain that acts like the command center of your brain’s reward system, the mesolimbic dopamine pathway. Its job is relatively simple. When something good happens- you get a new high score on your favourite game, or you get a compliment on your hair- it releases dopamine, a chemical neurotransmitter that labels the experience as “worth repeating again”. 
However, there’s a big problem with this circuit- it evolved long before smartphones existed and thus cannot differentiate a genuinely rewarding experience and a notification ping. Every like, comment, follow request, or streak reminder lights up the same neural pathway that lights up when you win money, eat your favourite snack, and most troublingly, when using drugs and alcohol (Sherman et al., 2025). Researchers at the London South Bank University who study this “dopa-mining” effect directly found that repeated engagement trains the brain to octave those hits, making it progressively harder to resist checking your phone (Kuss, 2025).
Dopamine hits aren’t the only thing shaping our reactions to our phones either. During adolescence, the brain undergoes a process called neural pruning, where it eliminates weaker or less-used synaptic connections while reinforcing and strengthening the ones you exercise the most, similar to how a gardener cuts back stray branches so the strongest ones can grow thicker. Neural pruning is a normal and, in fact, necessary process for our neurological development. However, it is experience-dependent – so whichever circuits are being used the most during these fundamental years of our growth are the ones that survive.
This means that when a teenager spends hours a day chasing quick dopamine hits from the constant buzz of notifications, those reward pathways are consolidated and strengthened while the circuits responsible for sustained attention and delayed gratification are pruned away from disuse (Sherman et al., 2025). 
Things only get harder from here because the part of the brain that’s supposed to apply the brakes isn’t ready yet. The prefrontal cortex, the part of the brain responsible for impulse control and weighing long-term consequences, doesn’t fully mature until the mid-twenties, whilst the amygdala, which processes emotions and social threat, is fully ready in teenage years. This awkward mismatch means that teenagers feel the all-too-strong pull of FOMO, social comparison and the anxiety of being left on delivered far more intensely than adults do, while also not having the ability to resist acting on it.
The effects of social media addiction have far deeper claws into our well-being than we realise. Teens who spend more than three hours a day on social media show measurably impaired impulse control, which closely mirrors the patterns seen in substance-related addictions ( Alam et al., 2025). Researchers describe this escalation in 2 stages- early use is driven by the immediate dopamine hit of likes and validation, but sustained, compulsive use is maintained by a completely different system- a breakdown in the pathways that link the prefrontal cortex to the limbic system leaves people scrolling not because it feels good, but to escape feeling bad (Zhang & Li, 2025). This phenomenon is called digital anhedonia- a diminished capacity to feel pleasure in real-world experiences after prolonged digital overstimulation (Rao, 2025).
None of this means that the only solution is to give up social media entirely, but understanding what goes on in your brain can change what you actually do about it. Turning off non-essential notifications removes a large share of the tiny dopamine hits that pull you back in. Protecting sleep and ensuring that social media does not interfere with your sleep schedule avoids worsening emotional regulation or academic performance. 
At the end of the day, you’re just a teenager whose brain is being expertly reverse-engineered by people who pick apart brains and how to manipulate them for a living- engineers, data scientists, and behavioural psychologists whose entire job is figuring out how to keep you scrolling for one more minute. That’s not a fair fight, and it’s not one you can win through sheer willpower alone. Understanding the science behind it simply puts a weapon in your hands- how you wield it is up to you.

title: US-Iranian Conflict
content:
The US-Iranian conflict has been ongoing since February 28, 2026, and has been deemed as a significant international conflict in modern history. As a battle originally revolved around Israel and the rising tensions in the Middle East, it has turned from a regional concern to a global one. Countries all around the world watch as the war unfolds.
As of August 11, 2026, the Iranian war has persisted and is still heavily impacting the market. The United States and Iran are in the midst of negotiations, but the parties have failed to come to an agreement.
The Strait of Hormuz is a choke point, as it is situated between the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman. Being placed in a critical position for trade, the Strait has 20% of the global petroleum going through that singular point, a connection from the Middle East to the rest of the world. In fact, in 2025, 20 million barrels of oil passed through this strait daily. Iran has created a blockade around the Strait, preventing any ships from passing. The impact is especially felt in Asian markets, with 90% of the oil from Iran going to Asia.
Oil prices have surged from around $70 a barrel before the war to a peak of over $120, and it is now stabilizing at around $83, roughly a 20% increase from the pre-war price. 
Nicknamed as “black gold”, oil is one of the most important raw materials in the economy today and has been for centuries. Oil is used for many of the products that consumers buy: most skincare products, fabrics in clothing, shoes, toys, and almost anything else you can think of that all have some form of petroleum (or a byproduct of it). 
Oil is a major player in the global economy, and when the price of oil is up, it increases consumer price, and therefore results in a reduction of disposable income for consumers. With less money circulating in the market, the economy begins to slow, and since more people are spending less, retailers would mark up prices to make up for the reduced amount of sales, contributing to inflation. When there was a breakdown in negotiations and a tightening of the naval blockade, the oil prices shot up, and the major indexes (S&P 500, Dow Jones, Nasdaq) have all followed a downtrend.
The US-Iranian War is classified as a macroeconomic event, as war commonly leads to the restriction of resources all halting the economy, and investors begin to go towards safer options. This includes options such as government bonds CDs, and liquidizing. Large international corporations, especially automotive companies like General Motors (GM) and Ford (F), begin to struggle, and they impose their profit loss on the consumers. 
Supply and demand run the world, as demonstrated by the conflict with Iran. Generally, wars have several impacts on the economy and government. The government would divert funding to war efforts, which would alter priorities from development, such as infrastructure, to the conflict. There would be a higher cost of living on average, a decrease in purchasing power, and a strain on the currency. Moreover, it can cause the Federal Reserve to hike up interest rates, which would reduce inflation but cause the cost of borrowing to increase. Increasing interest rates can, in turn, increase the cost of credit cards, housing, and car loans. Recently, the interest rate call from the Federal Reserve on July 29 still maintained an interest rate of 3.5% to 3.75%. 
While the US Stock Market has since been recovering and adapting to the war and its circumstances, the damage to infrastructure such as oil extraction sites will not be undone, so the aftermath of the conflict will still have a lingering impact on oil production (and therefore the rest of the economy). 
Iran has experienced sanctions from the United States for 50 years, and President Trump decided to continue with the sanction strategy by placing more into effect, which would further put pressure on the Iranian economy. However, sanctions also harm the country that applies them. In this case, the United States is reducing its oil imports from the Middle East and moving towards reserves and other countries for oil.
So what? Depending on the news, your investments would likely follow the market. With bad news like the breaking down of peace talks, the Strait of Hormuz will persist as a pain in the economies around the world, and as the world begins to run out of oil from other sources, it can lead to recessions and dire consequences. As people begin to be frugal with their money, there are fewer larger purchases, especially cars that need gas to run, making the economy suffer.

title: Understand Passkeys: The Tech Behind Passwordless Sign-ins
content:
A Forbes Advisor survey of 2,000 Americans found that 46% had a password stolen in the past year, and on average people reuse the same password across at least four different accounts. Nearly a third of respondents blamed password reuse for their own account getting hacked. That’s the danger of passwords in a nutshell: one leaked password can unlock several parts of someone’s digital life at once.
That’s the problem passkeys were built to solve. This article breaks down what a passkey actually is, how it works under the hood, why it’s considered safer than a password, and where this technology is headed.
What Exactly Is a Passkey?
A passkey is a sign-in method that lets you log into an app or website without typing a username and password. Instead, you unlock your phone, laptop, or security key the same way you always do: with your face, your fingerprint, or a PIN; and that’s it. You’re in.
The FIDO Alliance, the industry group behind the technology, describes a passkey simply as a FIDO authentication credential that lets a user sign in to apps and websites with the same process they use to unlock their device. In plain words: no more secret words to remember, type, or steal.
A simple way to remember the difference:
Password = something you know (a secret you memorized)
Passkey = something you have (your device) + something you are (your fingerprint or face)
That combination is exactly why passkeys are considered so much harder to steal than a plain password.
How Does a Passkey Actually Work?
This is where it gets interesting, but don’t worry, the concept is simple once you see it laid out.
When you create a passkey for a website, your device generates two mathematically linked keys:
A public key, which gets sent to and stored on the website’s server.
A private key, which never leaves your device.
Because passkeys use end-to-end encryption, not even the companies creating them can see or change them. The public key is basically useless on its own – a hacker could steal it from a company’s database and still not be able to log into your account with it.
Here’s what happens each time you sign in:
You visit the website and choose to sign in with a passkey.
The website sends a random “challenge” to your device.
Your device asks you to confirm it’s really you – usually with Face ID, a fingerprint, or your device PIN.
Once confirmed, your device uses the private key to “sign” that challenge and sends the signed response back.
The website checks the signature against the public key it already has on file. If it matches, you’re logged in.
Your fingerprint or face scan never actually leaves your device. It’s only used locally to unlock the private key. The website never sees your biometric data – it only receives a mathematical proof that the check succeeded.
This is also why passkeys are considered phishing-resistant. Since the passkey only works with the website that created it, even if you get tricked into clicking a fake login link that looks identical to the real site, your device simply won’t offer up the passkey for the wrong website. There’s nothing to type, so there’s nothing to “trick” out of you.
Where Did Passkeys Come From?
Passkeys aren’t a brand-new invention that appeared overnight. The idea first took hold in 2009, when Validity Sensors and PayPal jointly developed the concept of using biometrics instead of passwords for online identification. A few years later, several tech leaders founded the FIDO (Fast Identity Online) Alliance in July 2012 to build open standards around this idea.
Things really picked up in 2022, when Apple, Google, and Microsoft – normally competitors – jointly committed to supporting passkeys across their platforms. Since then, adoption has grown fast. According to FIDO Alliance research, 53% of people reported enabling passkeys on at least one of their accounts, with 22% enabling them on every account they possibly can. On the business side, a FIDO Alliance survey found that 87% of decision-makers surveyed had already deployed passkeys at their organizations.
Are Passkeys Actually More Secure Than Passwords?
Short answer: yes, significantly. 
Here’s the side-by-side comparison:
Feature	Passwords	Passkeys
What it relies on	A secret string you memorize	A cryptographic key pair tied to your device
Phishing risk	High – can be typed into fake sites	Very low – only works on the real website
Reuse across sites	Common (and risky)	Impossible – always unique per site
What a data breach exposes	The actual password (or its hash)	Only a public key, which is useless alone
Speed of logging in	Typing + possibly a 2FA code	One tap, glance, or fingerprint scan
Security researchers back this up with numbers. The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre notes that its own technical analysis demonstrates that passkeys are always as secure or more secure than two-step verification using the strongest password. And it’s not just about safety – it’s about speed too. Passkey logins can be up to eight times faster than signing in with a username, password, and a 2FA code.
But “more secure” isn’t just a vague claim – it comes down to a few specific weaknesses that passwords have and passkeys simply don’t:
Passwords are a shared secret; passkeys aren’t. For a password to work, both you and the website’s server have to know the same secret string. That means it has to travel across the internet and sit in a database somewhere – two separate points where it can leak. A passkey’s private key never leaves your device and is never transmitted anywhere, not even during login.
Passwords can be typed, so they can be stolen mid-typing. Keyloggers, someone glancing at your screen, or malware watching your clipboard can all capture a password the moment you enter it. A passkey is approved with a fingerprint or face scan – there’s no string of characters to intercept in the first place.
Passwords depend on human memory; passkeys don’t. People create weak, guessable passwords because they have to remember them. The Forbes Advisor survey found that over a third of people write their passwords down on paper, and some even share them with friends or family. Passkeys are generated automatically by cryptographic algorithms, so there’s no “weak password” for a person to accidentally choose.
A leaked company database is far less dangerous. If a company gets hacked, its password database (even if hashed) can sometimes still be cracked. A passkey database only contains public keys, which are useless without the matching private key – so a breach on the company’s end doesn’t put your account at risk.
Credential stuffing stops working entirely. This is when hackers take a list of leaked username-password pairs from one breach and try them on other sites, betting that people reused the password. Since every passkey is unique to the site it was created for, there’s no reusable credential to try elsewhere.
Because there’s no password sitting in a database anywhere, a big category of attacks simply stops working. Credential stuffing (reusing leaked passwords across sites), phishing pages that harvest your login, and brute-force guessing attacks all lose their main target once passwords are gone.
Passkeys vs. Traditional Two-Factor Authentication (2FA)
You might be thinking, “Isn’t this basically what 2FA already does?” Not quite. Traditional 2FA (like getting a text message code) adds a second layer on top of a password that can still be phished, guessed, or leaked. A passkey replaces the password entirely, and the whole process is resistant to phishing by design rather than as an add-on.
That said, passkeys and biometrics are related but not identical. Your face or fingerprint is only used locally to unlock your device and approve the use of a stored key – it’s never transmitted anywhere, and no company ever holds a copy of your biometric data.
Real-World Applications
Passkeys have moved well beyond theory. Some places you’re already likely to encounter them:
Big tech accounts. Google made passkeys the default sign-in option for its accounts. Apple, Microsoft, GitHub, Amazon, and many others support them too.
Everyday apps and retailers. Companies like Instacart, Kayak, Verizon, CVS Health, and Nintendo now offer passkey sign-in.
Payments. This is one of the more exciting frontiers. Mastercard’s Payment Passkey Service lets shoppers confirm an online purchase with a fingerprint or face scan instead of typing a card number or a one-time code, aiming for true one-click checkout.
Government services. Public agencies are experimenting too – the U.S. state of Michigan implemented passkeys on its login portal and saw 1,300 fewer password-reset calls in a single month.
The benefits go beyond convenience for users. Organizations that switch to passkeys also see real business results, including a 50% reduction in login abandonment for Air New Zealand and a 98% reduction in mobile account takeover fraud for CVS Health. Fewer forgotten passwords also means fewer costly support tickets for IT and help desk teams.
But…. What Happens If You Lose Your Device?
This is a fair worry, and it’s the most common question people have. The good news: losing your phone doesn’t mean losing your accounts forever.
Most passkeys are “synced”, meaning they’re backed up through your credential manager, such as iCloud Keychain, Google Password Manager, or a third-party app like Proton Pass or Bitwarden. If you get a new device and sign back into that same account, your passkeys reappear automatically. There’s also cross-device sign-in: your phone can act as an authenticator for a laptop nearby, verified using Bluetooth to confirm proximity.
For extra caution, some services also let you store a passkey on a dedicated hardware security key (like a YubiKey), which never syncs to the cloud and stays fully under your physical control.
Current Limitations
Passkeys aren’t perfect yet, and it’s worth being honest about that:
Not every site supports them. Adoption is growing fast, but plenty of smaller websites still only offer passwords.
Older devices may not work. Passkeys need a reasonably modern operating system and browser that support the WebAuthn standard.
Switching ecosystems can be clunky. Moving passkeys from an Android phone to an iPhone (or the reverse) isn’t always seamless, though cross-platform credential managers are closing this gap.
Recovery still matters. If you lose every device that holds a copy of your passkey and never set up a backup method, getting back into your account can be a hassle.
Because of these gaps, passwords haven’t disappeared completely — yet. Security agencies like the NCSC still recommend using a strong, unique password with 2FA turned on for any account that doesn’t yet support passkeys.
So,… What About The Future? Will Passwords Disappear?
The direction is pretty clear. Every major tech company – Apple, Google, Microsoft, Amazon, Meta – is investing heavily in passkeys, and government cybersecurity agencies are actively encouraging citizens to switch whenever the option is available. As more websites, banks, and apps add support, the everyday experience of “logging in” is quietly changing from typing to tapping.
Full replacement of passwords won’t happen overnight. It will likely be a gradual shift – a few more services turning on passkey support every month, more people getting comfortable with the concept, and passwords slowly becoming the backup option instead of the main one. But the trend line points in one direction: fewer things to remember, fewer things to steal, and a safer, faster way to prove it’s really you.

title: David Chou’s Journey
content:
About David Chou
“My name is David Chou. I am the owner here at Motorenn. I founded this company with my business partner, Austin. I went to the United States Military Academy, West Point, where I got a Bachelor of Science in mechanical engineering. I later earned my MBA at MIT, as well as my Master’s in mechanical engineering. A key to my business development was spending a couple of years at McKinsey & Co.”
Finding the Right Business Idea
As with many business ventures, it is best to have it grounded in some experiences that you’ve had or passions that you’ve had. We have seen successes come from sources of strength, and people who are unsuccessful tend to do it in something that they are not confident about.
I have done a lot of work in the automotive industry. I managed corporate strategy at Edmunds.com, then at Carmax, which is the US’s largest used car retailer. It gave me an appreciation for how the used auto industry worked. I was also a major car enthusiast. Growing up, supercars and sports cars were always very exciting for me.
Mirroring all that together, it came down to: “Hey, we can open up our own kind of online, used car dealership, but focus on the exotic sports car, luxury car segment, and bring in a really cool new experience of things.”
The Power of Passion
Absolutely. I think it does because entrepreneurship is very hard. It is extremely hard. People who are really good at it have to have a lot of dedication, flexibility and intellectual curiosity, and endurance, and that is hard if you don’t have passion for the subject.
If you are just doing it because it just makes money, that’s fine, but it is hard to be super successful because when you get tested, you have to have resolve. I think if it is something that you really care about, you have more resolve in trying to figure it out.
Financial Challenges in Starting a Business
I’d say the number one issue of building a business early on is money. Business classes tend not to really teach you how to start a business. You need money, and how you get that money comes from a variety of ways.
One, you saved it yourself, you work a normal career for a couple of years, maybe tens of years. You self-fund, and you have an idea that works. You test the idea. That is always the best: testing the idea before you leave your financial security somewhere else.
Some people can get business loans. Those are very hard to get unless you have a track record. Even if you’re smart, you have a 4.0 GPA, Valedictorian, scholarships, all that doesn’t mean anything to Chase Bank. Chase Bank cares if you’re the principal engineer at Google, working on some kind of 3D glasses widget, and now you’re trying to start a business selling 3D glasses on your own. That’s a real financial track record they will loan against.
Another way is friends and family. At the end of the day, it’s good to be born in the right family. It just is what it is. Having a rich uncle, a rich mom, and a dad who helps out. But it doesn’t mean you’ll be successful, because if you don’t go with the right approach, you’re just going to waste that money.
Getting that money is very, very hard. You have to be smart when you do that. Make sure you have a good idea. It’s based on experience or some real intuition. But ideally, you can test it before you cut the cord and just focus on it completely. You don’t want to be leaving a job that’s putting food on the table, especially as you’re older and you have a family to support.
Importance of Financial Literacy
I think having good financial literacy becomes more and more important the more complicated your business is. If you bought an apple for a dollar and you sell an apple for two dollars, I made a dollar. It’s pretty straightforward.
But as you get to a more complicated business and now you’re employing people and now you’re making big investments, having a couple of courses where you really understand what are some of the ways to think about how money moves becomes very important.
Understanding the difference between gross profit and operating profit, how much money do you actually make at the end of things, not accounting for interest? If you borrowed money from the bank, you have to pay interest. That interest doesn’t really show how good your business is, but it still costs you money. You want to know both numbers. What does EBIT look like? What does EBITA look like?
If you’re learning those terms, those are terms that you live with in the business world. Knowing all that helps you manage a more and more complicated business.
Key Financial Metrics
Every business is going to be different. If you are doing a tech startup and you fundraise and you have Venture Capital funding, they expect you to show customer growth, usage growth. You need to know what your funders are looking for and make sure you’re delivering on that.
In my business, we deal with car sales. It’s very important for us to know what our costs are for the cars. What are our repair costs on those cars? How long does it take us to sell those cars? All of that goes into just how much money we’re actually making on a routine basis with these cars.
Just make sure that the metrics you look at make sense to measure success. If it’s not measuring success, it’s not a useful metric. It has to be measurable, and it has to be something that you can control.
Managing Investor Relationships
We raised a little bit with venture capitalists. They check in with us every quarter or so, but now that Venture Capital is kind of focused on AI in particular, and we’re not really AI-focused, we’re kind of not raising any more of them. They will have their metrics. They will say, “Hey, look, we want to see how many users you’re getting, how much revenue you’re generating, what does that growth percentage look like?”
We also have friends and family investors. That’s the easiest. Borrowing some money from your uncle or your mom or dad, especially because they believe in you. You want to show them that you can do something with the family money. There’s a level of trust there.
It’s about having good awareness and then just being a good communicator and staying ahead of things. It’s better to communicate bad news early, to communicate good news early. I think that is how you can stay pretty healthy in your relationship with the investors.
Managing Cash Flow
In terms of just managing cash flow, who’s more interested in where the money is going but you? You put the money to start the business. You put the blood, sweat, and tears to start the business. None of your employees will ever be as interested.
It’s about having the right software in place. We use QuickBooks. Managing that, staying on top of the bookkeeping, making sure you’re tracking the receipts – it feels like a chore, and it is a chore, and it stinks. It’s not fun to do. It’s probably the least fun part of the job, but you still need to do it.
As you get larger, you hire help. You want to make sure you’re hiring good help – people who are good bookkeepers and accountants, and staying on top of it, and who are trustworthy. It’s also trust but verify. Always be on top of it.
When you’re dealing with rapid growth, it’s telling you, “Hey, it’s a boom time.” But it’s also dangerous that you can overgrow. I think a lot of businesses overgrew in the post-COVID boom. When the crash came, they couldn’t stop fast enough, and that hurt a lot.
If your business can’t make money when things are bad, then you don’t have a very good business at all. Understand what your business is. Know what you can cut, what is the core to the business, and is that core business sustainable in chaos?
Advice for Young Entrepreneurs
The world is changing a lot. For somebody with the right drive, with the right capability, and good emotional intelligence and overall intelligence, there’s a lot of opportunity out there. But go about it smartly. Think it through. Don’t just dive out there and just do it.
Have a good idea of what you’re trying to do, have a good product fit, and then know where your finances are coming from. You can have all that together, then you have a good shot. Because this world is tough, even some of the best people will fail. You can be a really good business person and still fail.
There is no shame in doing a business and then saying, “Hey, I need to go back and get a job.” That’s just life. The key is we’re all trying to live a good life. We have to make smart decisions throughout all of that.
Advice for High School Students
Think about the career path you’re looking to do. That career path will start shutting down on you sooner than you expect. The older you get, the harder it is to make that change. The younger you start in something that you know you can just excel fantastically at, the more money you’re going to make.
If you’re coming from a family business perspective and your parents own some kind of shop that you are probably going to inherit and you don’t hate it, think about classes that will really help your business that you already know. You probably need to take more classes on the trade itself, but you need to understand how finances work.
If you don’t have any family business and you want to go the high-powered business way, you’re aiming to go to Goldman Sachs or McKenzie, BCG, Bane. That’s about getting straight A’s, a 1600 on the SAT, going to UCLA, MIT, Stanford, and then excelling at those interviews.
Then there’s the aspect of going and figuring something out. Learn things that excite you. Most successful entrepreneurs are the ones who do things that they’re excited about. Learn something you’re excited about, that has a real application, where you can really be a master of the subject matter that can really propel you.
The Value of Higher Education
You do not need higher education to succeed necessarily. But I would highly recommend it. I have employed people who are just really good at making money and doing things, especially for sales. Your EQ can be super high, and you don’t learn EQ at Harvard.
But running your business and doing sales as a part of business are two very different things. If you want to actually run the business, it is really good to have education. Especially if you’re going into it fresh.
I would caution against just taking a lot of money, starting a business with zero educational background. Does not mean that you have to go to Harvard, but the point is to educate yourself, know how to run the business, know how to read financials, know the subject you are doing. Know that you will be way more successful than if you are just sitting on the couch at home.
What to Look for in Employees
I think there are probably two ways to think about employees. First is personality fit. You want to make sure you get people that you get along with. They got to be good. But if your personalities clash, that is not a good start for anything. Make sure there is a good cultural fit for what your product is, what your company is, and what your customers expect.
Second, are they good at what they do? For some roles, you just want somebody who is good at that role, like a bookkeeper. But there are other roles where you might be more open to someone who is a good intellectual athlete. They are smart. They are driven. I look for people who are good salespeople, period. And they have good energy, and they are smart.
Marketing and Social Media
When I think about advertising, it is very business-dependent. Think about what your business needs and where your customers are. For us, we are in the luxury car segment. We list all the car listing sites. We are constantly auditing them. Are they effective for us? Are people using them?
I always approach advertisers thinking about how they are making money for me, and how they are being effective for me. You can always say no. They always upsell you on things. I would always approach things with a sense of, let me test if this makes sense before spending a lot of money on it.
We’re always measuring every channel that we think of as marketing. Every marketing channel needs to be ROI effective for us, and that is how you should think about it too.

title: The Growing World of Cybercrime
content:
In today’s interconnected world, where you chat with friends or share memes with just a few clicks, knowing how to stay safe online is more important than ever. Even though you may think that you are knowledgeable enough to stay safe online, a study found that one in three individuals will be affected by cybersecurity threats on their devices, with most of them not even noticing!
Cyberattacks don’t care who you are or where you come from. They can affect anyone, whether you’re a kid, an adult, or a big company, resulting in devastating consequences including: 
Theft of Confidential Information: Your personal details, like passwords and email addresses, may be stolen
Financial Loss: You could lose your money or be forced to pay for damages caused by the cyberattack
Identity Theft: Individuals might pretend to be you and ruin your reputation both on social media and in real life.
Computer Meltdown: Your devices may stop functioning normally due to the damage caused by the attack
A recent example of a widespread cyberattack occurred on the platform TikTok – a website that needs no introduction as it’s used by millions of individuals all across the world. Although TikTok has been taking several measures to secure its website due to the several data breaches that it has experienced since August 2020, users were hit especially hard this June.

TikTok has been the victim of several cyberattacks recently, resulting in personal data being stolen from millions of individuals
Hackers exploited the website’s vulnerabilities and sent malicious links to several users, exposing the data and personal information of over 285 million individuals. Stolen information included:
Names
Ages
Gender
Profile Images
Email Addresses
Phone Numbers
Facial Recognition Data
Other Personal Information
Worst of all, many users don’t even know that their information was stolen, meaning that hackers may be exploiting their data to cause financial loss, while the victim remains unaware of any harm they may be experiencing. 
It doesn’t take much for hackers to cause damage to your identity and well-being, even something as simple as an email address or phone number could be used to gain access to your confidential information. 
Sadly, this is only the beginning of a never-ending list of cyberattacks, including the CrowdStrike data breach, Sony PlayStation Network Attack, T-Mobile Data Breach, Uber Data Leak, and many more. The most concerning part is that the number of these issues is climbing – according to Forbes, attacks have risen by 71% over the past few years. 

With the increase in Cyberattacks, a study found that one in Three Individuals will experience cybersecurity threats on their devices!
However, most of these threats can be prevented. As a matter of fact, a study finds that human error is the cause of 95% of cybersecurity problems, meaning it is crucial to be educated about staying safe online. By learning how to avoid common mistakes, everyone can stay protected online from dangerous attacks.
Specifically, it is important to educate and protect young teenagers because they are the most susceptible to attacks. In fact, an article found that 72% of young children have experienced a cyber threat online over the past year. 

Techinance is a non-profit offering free courses with the aim to educate individuals regarding cyber safety. 
Thankfully, nonprofits like Techinance were created with the aim to empower the youth through education, offering a free course on Cyber Security including:
Introduction to Cybersecurity: An introduction to the fundamentals of cybersecurity and its importance in the digital age
The World of Cybercrime: Understand the different types of cybercrime and the dangers they pose
Safe Online Practices: Be equipped with the knowledge and skills to stay safe and avoid being vulnerable to cyberattacks
Digital Footprint and Privacy: Learn the concept of digital footprints and strategies for protecting personal information online
Career Opportunities: An exploration of career opportunities in cybersecurity and similar fields
And much, much more!
